claims.text: Several thousand years later, he led the Vanyar of the Host of the West to Middle-earth to fight in the War of Wrath at the end of the First Age.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Lost Road and Other Writings, "Part Two: Valinor and Middle-earth before The Lord of the Rings, VI. Quenta Silmarillion", p. 326
J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part One. Time and Ageing: XVII. Generational Schemes", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021, p. 128

claims.text:
The name Ingwion was changed from an earlier form Ingwiel, which was itself changed from Ingwil. The meanings of these earlier forms are unclear, but they all contain the name of his father Ingwë as one of their elements.
However, in The Nature of Middle-earth, from a text dating c. 1959, the form Ingwil reappears again.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part Two. The Later Quenta Silmarillion: The Last Chapters of the Quenta Silmarillion", p. 246; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Shaping of Middle-earth, "VII. The Earliest Annals of Beleriand: Notes [to text AB I]", note 68, p. 313; J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part One. Time and Ageing: XVII. Generational Schemes", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021, p. 128

claims.text: There, Ingwiel, the "prince of all the Elves", was the commander of the force that landed and captured the haven of Eglarest (in the text it was called Eglorest) in one of the first battles of the war, driving away the Orcs from the shore.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Lost Road and Other Writings, "Part Two: Valinor and Middle-earth before The Lord of the Rings, III. The Later Annals of Beleriand", pp. 143-4
